signal.title: cilium-cli: don't count pods rejected before running as live
signal.text: The AKS connectivity test setup failed with "unexpected number of other node pods: 2" on a cluster that had already recovered: a node had gone under DiskPressure, kubelet evicted the pods bound to it, and listing pods by label selector returns those terminal leftovers alongside the healthy replacement. The echo pod count now skips pods that were rejected before ever running. WaitForDeployment already ran for the same deployments and stays authoritative, and a container that ran and crashed has an empty pod-level reason so it is still counted and still reported. The DaemonSet wait hit the same eviction burst but cannot be fixed by filtering, since a rejected pod really does mean a replica is missing. kubelet's rejection backoff reaches about four minutes, which the five minute timeout cannot outlast, so it gave up a minute after the node was healthy again. It now polls for a bounded grace period past the timeout, but only while every failed pod was rejected before running, and names those pods in the error. Node disk usage was invisible in the sysdump, so the last commit collects nodefs and imagefs per node along with the DiskPressure condition. This PR was prepared with AIL:3.
signal.author: aanm

signal.title: hubble: correlate policy for audit verdicts and implicit denies
signal.text: `CorrelatePolicy` currently handles forwarded/redirected flows and drops with `DropReason_POLICY_DENY`, but misses two categories: **Audit verdicts** — `Verdict_AUDIT` (code 4) represents traffic that was allowed because the matching policy is in audit mode, but *would have been denied* otherwise. These flows hit the early return and never get correlated, so `hubble observe` shows the audit verdict without any associated policy in the `*DeniedBy` fields. **Implicit denies** — `DropReason_POLICY_DENIED` (code 133) covers the default-deny case where no allow rule matched. Only `DropReason_POLICY_DENY` (code 181, explicit deny rule) was checked. In practice, most deny-by-default setups produce code 133 drops, and all of those were silently skipped. This adds `Verdict_AUDIT` as an `audited` flow category that populates `*DeniedBy` (since it represents what would be denied), and extends the `denied` check to cover both `POLICY_DENY` and `POLICY_DENIED` drop reasons. Tests added for audit flows at both egress/ingress and implicit deny (`POLICY_DENIED`) at both directions. There is a third aspect to #42044 around `PolicyMatchNone` (match_type 0 for implicit denies where there is genuinely no single rule to point at) — that is a deeper design question around what `lookupPolicyForKey` should return, left for a separate discussion. Fixes: #42044

signal.title: hubble: Add Kubernetes Pod UID to flow endpoints
signal.text: Hubble currently identifies a Pod mainly by cluster, namespace, and name. Kubernetes permits a deleted object's name to be reused, while its UID identifies that specific object lifetime. This matters especially for StatefulSet Pods, but applies to any recreated Pod. Adding the UID improves flow attribution. Consumers can distinguish Pod instances and correlate flows with Kubernetes records keyed by UID. The UID is carried through IPCache and ClusterMesh metadata, so Hubble can expose it for remote endpoints when that metadata is available. Cilium also uses the UID internally: - IPCache deletion checks UID, preventing a delayed Pod, CEP, or CES deletion from removing metadata belonging to a replacement Pod. - Same-name Pod replacements update IPCache, cgroup, endpoint, and host-network state. IPCache and NOTRACK changes install new state before removing old state, allowing a short overlap instead of a gap. - Kubernetes drop events use the UID captured in the flow instead of resolving whichever Pod currently owns that namespace/name. The UID remains optional when metadata is unavailable or components are running mixed versions. This PR was prepared with AIL:4. Codex drafted the implementation and tests. I reviewed the code and changed the replacement handling. ```release-note Hubble flow endpoints now include the Kubernetes Pod UID. ```

signal.title: mac: Make `mac.MAC` a `[6]byte`
signal.text: This PR migrates `pkg/mac.MAC` from being a [`net.HardwareAddr`](https://pkg.go.dev/net#HardwareAddr) (which is a `[]byte`) to being a `[6]byte`. Why we can do this: `net.HardwareAddr` has to be a slice because it has to support MAC address representations under different formats/size, such as the 20-octet IP over InfiniBand link-layer one. Cilium has always been stricter in the MAC addresses it accepts and already enforced the IEEE 802 MAC-48 format (see `mac.MAC`'s existing docstring: "MAC address is an net.HardwareAddr encapsulation to force cilium to only use MAC-48.") What we gain from doing this: We already wanted MAC-48-only format before, now this is guaranteed and enforced by the type itself, meaning we don't need to validate the value in as many places because once we have a valid `mac.MAC`, we know it's a 48 MAC. Switching from a slice to an array also means `MAC` becomes comparable (`m1 == m2`) and can be used as map keys (`map[mac.MAC]string` for example). From a memory point of view, an array is also better than a slice, but at this scale, the gain is probably not measurable. Overall, `[6]byte` is to `net.HardwareAddr` what `netip.Addr`/`netip.Prefix` are to `net.IP`/`net.IPNet`.

signal.title: ipcache: max_entries is hard-coded at 512k with no configuration path, blocks clusters beyond ~500k routable IPs
signal.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? **Description** cilium_ipcache_v2 is created with a hard-coded capacity of 512,000 entries (MaxEntries in pkg/maps/ipcache/ipcache.go, propagated to the datapath as IPCACHE_MAP_SIZE). Unlike most other large BPF maps, there is no CLI flag to override it, and --bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio does not cover it. Since the ipcache holds one entry per routable IP (pods, nodes, CIDR/FQDN identities), this constant is a hard ceiling on cluster size: at ~10k nodes with a realistic pod density, the map saturates. When the map is full, upserts fail with ENOSPC and the entry is dropped (a warn log is the only signal). Traffic to/from the affected IPs is then misclassified, which at minimum breaks policy enforcement for those endpoints. We are targeting cluster size that already hit this limit in scale testing. **What we observed (scale test)** Scale test on a setup, 10k virtual nodes, ~700k pods target, Cilium : Agent logs — upserts silently lost: ``` time=2026-07-20T21:57:41Z level=warn msg="unable to update bpf map" module=agent.datapath.ipcache-bpf-listener ipAddr="{IP:10.6.155.145 Mask:ffffffff}" identity="{Source:custom-resource ID:43285 ...}" modification=Upsert error="update map cilium_ipcache_v2: update: no space left on device" ``` Map confirmed full on the node: ``` # bpftool map show id 331 331: lpm_trie name cilium_ipcache_ flags 0x81 key 24B value 24B max_entries 512000 memlock 43008000B # bpftool map dump id 331 | grep -c "key:" 512000 ``` Note the memory numbers: the full map accounts for 43 MB of kernel memory (84 B/entry), on a node with 3.7 GiB available. Memory is not the constraint; max_entries alone is. Environment: Cilium v1.18.5, kernel > 6.8.x, 10k virtual nodes, ~700k pods target. **Precedent exists, including for LPM tries.** Three LPM-trie map families are already size-configurable through the exact mechanism we are proposing: the egress gateway policy maps (--egress-gateway-policy-map-max -> EGRESS_POLICY_MAP_SIZE), the per-endpoint policy map, an LPM trie since the wildcard-ports rework (--bpf-policy-map-max -> POLICY_MAP_SIZE, wired in pkg/maps/policymap/cell.go), and the LB source-range maps (--bpf-lb-source-range-map-max -> LB4/LB6_SRC_RANGE_MAP_SIZE, falling back to --bpf-lb-map-max). Same flag pattern for hash maps: --bpf-node-map-max, --bpf-auth-map-max, etc. ### Describe the feature you'd like We'd like the ipcache map size to be configurable, e.g. via a --bpf-ipcache-map-max agent flag defaulting to the current 512,000, following the exact pattern already used for the egress gateway policy map, the per-endpoint policy map, and the LB source-range maps (all LPM tries, see precedent in the previous section). Raising it is what stands between us and 10,000-node clusters. We've done our best to reason from the code and git history, but that only goes so far, there may be context (past incidents, discussions, design intent) that isn't visible from us or we may have missed. That's really what we're hoping to learn here: - Is there a structural reason (verifier, datapath, operational) for the 512k ceiling that we're missing? ### Notify relevant community channels _No response_ ### (Optional) Describe your proposed solution _No response_

signal.title: fix(bpf): don't drop IPv6 RS/RAs when masquerading
signal.text: Please ensure your pull request adheres to the following guidelines: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [ ] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! `snat_v6_nat()` punts ICMPv6 echo replies, redirects and NS/NA to the stack but returns `DROP_NAT_UNSUPP_PROTO` for every other type, so Router Solicitations and Advertisements do not survive the egress masquerade path: ``` xx drop (Unsupported protocol for NAT masquerade, -1) flow 0x0 , file nodeport_egress.h:152, identity host->unknown: fe80::bae9:24ff:fe80:ebfe -> ff02::1 icmp RouterAdvertisement ``` This hits a node whose only IPv6 address is a link-local. RS/RA are always sourced from a link-local, and when no selected device has a global IPv6 address the best IPv6 fallback node address is the link-local itself — `fallbackAddresses.update()` ranks candidates by public-vs-private and scope, and does not exclude link-locals — so `bpfMasqAddrs()` hands that address to the datapath as `nat_ipv6_masquerade`. `__snat_v6_needs_masquerade()` then matches such a packet on its very first test, source equals the masquerade address, and answers `NAT_NEEDED`. That leaves `snat_v6_nat()` nothing but the ICMPv6 type to go on: it only consults `snat_v6_nat_can_skip()` for TCP/UDP/SCTP. Neighbor Discovery is link-local by definition and must never be masqueraded — rewriting an RA's source would advertise the masquerade address as the router's link-local. RFC 4890 section 4.4, which 5244b68c1468 ("bpf: Hande icmpv6 in host firewall") cites when it added the NS/NA punt, lists RS/RA in the same must-not-be-dropped group. Punt them to the stack alongside NS/NA, and cover both types with a BPF masquerade test for a node whose masquerade address is a link-local. Split out of #47394 so it can be reviewed and merged on its own; it is a standalone datapath fix that does not depend on the rest of that series. Fixes: #48093 ```release-note Fix IPv6 Router Solicitations and Router Advertisements being dropped with "Unsupported protocol for NAT masquerade" on nodes whose BPF masquerade address is a link-local address. ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally verified the drop in a live cluster, traced the masquerade address selection through `fallbackAddresses.update()`/`bpfMasqAddrs()`, confirmed the RFC 4890 §4.4 citation, and reviewed and ran the new BPF test.

signal.title: gateway-api: same-port HTTPS and TLS passthrough listeners are rejected on any SNI overlap, including a wildcard HTTPS listener next to an exact passthrough hostname
signal.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? Since v1.19.6 / v1.20.0, an HTTPS/Terminate listener and a TLS/Passthrough listener on the same port are marked `Conflicted=True/ProtocolConflict` whenever their hostnames intersect (`listenerPairConflict` on main, `samePortCrossProtocolConflictedListeners` on v1.19). So `*.example.com` (HTTPS) next to `api.example.com` (TLS passthrough) on 443 gets both listeners `Accepted=False`, and on 1.20 both are dropped from Envoy (#47306, #47457). This worked up to v1.19.5, so for the v1.19 branch it is also a regression: a config that 1.19.5 accepted and served stopped being accepted in the 1.19.6 patch release. #32292 is the same shape (`*.test` HTTPS + `proxmox.test` passthrough on 443), reproduced by a maintainer and accepted, and Envoy picks the exact `server_names` chain over the wildcard one. What actually broke was two listeners with the same hostname (two filter chains with the same match). The #44889 review asked to reject that same-hostname pair; the intersect predicate also caught the wildcard-superset case, and nothing tested it: the scenario matrix has same-port disjoint hostnames (works) and same-port same hostname (rejected), nothing in between. #47590 hit it on 1.20.0 and was closed after the reporter withdrew, so it was never discussed on its own. Why I care (Cozystack, cozystack/cozystack#3912): one Gateway with one address per tenant; on 443 a wildcard `*.<apex>` HTTPS listener for apps plus passthrough listeners for `api.<apex>` (management kube-apiserver, passthrough so clients see the real cert), `vm-exportproxy.<apex>` and `cdi-uploadproxy.<apex>`. One address per tenant is a hard constraint (every Gateway wants 443, so LB-IPAM sharing is out), and `api.<apex>:443` is in every kubeconfig. With the intersect rule we have to drop the wildcard and render one HTTPS listener per hostname under the 64-listener cap. Works, but a wildcard next to a more specific listener is exactly what the spec's hostname precedence rule is for. ### Describe the feature you'd like Conflict a same-port HTTPS/Terminate + TLS/Passthrough pair only when the normalized hostnames are equal (both catch-all included), the case Envoy can't disambiguate. For a strict wildcard superset (`*.example.com` vs `api.example.com`) apply the spec's "exact matches MUST be processed before wildcard matches" and accept both, as two HTTPS listeners with those hostnames on one port are accepted today. That keeps the #44889 same-hostname rejection and makes the cross-protocol branch match the same-protocol one. The spec lets an implementation call HTTPS and TLS on one port incompatible, so against the spec this is a request, not a conformance bug. Against v1.19 it is a regression fix, so I'd also ask for a backport there. Cilium already mixes the two protocols on one port for disjoint hostnames, and Envoy expresses the precedence. ### Notify relevant community channels @cilium/sig-servicemesh ### (Optional) Describe your proposed solution In `listenerPairConflict` (`operator/pkg/gateway-api/gateway_reconcile.go`; `listenersHaveSamePortCrossProtocolHostnameConflict` on v1.19/v1.20): conflict when `normalizedListenerHostname(first) == normalizedListenerHostname(second)`, otherwise not, same as the same-protocol branch below it. Translation already emits both filter chains on one listener and the matcher picks the exact server name first. Plus a test scenario for same port, wildcard HTTPS, exact passthrough, traffic to both names, and a re-check of `tlsroute-mixed-protocol-listeners`. I can do the PR if you want it; I'd rather agree on the rule here first.

signal.title: feat(bgp): support BGP unnumbered peering (RFC 5549 / ENHE)
signal.text: Depends on: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/47971, and https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/48094 - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [x] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer's Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! ## Description Adds interface-only ("unnumbered") BGP peering (RFC 5549 / ENHE) to the Cilium BGP control plane, driven through the `autoDiscovery` stanza on a peer. No `peerAddress` is configured: gobgp discovers the peer's IPv6 link-local address via ND on the interface and derives the local link-local source. This lets a Cilium node peer with a directly attached router (our case: FRR on a ToR) over a point-to-point link that carries no addressing beyond link-local. The interface can be named explicitly: ```yaml peers: - name: tor-switch peerASN: 65000 autoDiscovery: mode: Unnumbered unnumbered: interface: enp193s0f0np0 peerConfigRef: name: cilium-peer ``` For a fleet where the interface is not named the same everywhere — predictable names encode hardware location and change with the NIC model and driver, so one cluster config cannot name it, and pinning it with `CiliumBGPNodeConfigOverride` means one override object per node. For this case, we can discover using the default gateway: ```yaml peers: - name: tor-switch peerASN: 65000 autoDiscovery: mode: Unnumbered defaultGateway: addressFamily: ipv4 # "ipv4" or "ipv6" peerConfigRef: name: cilium-peer ``` Exactly one of `unnumbered` and `defaultGateway` is required with mode `Unnumbered`, enforced by CEL. In the `defaultGateway` form, only the *egress interface* of the default route is taken from the route — the peer address still comes from gobgp's ND on that interface. Two consequences worth calling out for review: - `addressFamily` selects which default route to follow, not the family the session runs over. The session is always IPv6 link-local, so following the IPv4 default route is a valid configuration. - Because the gateway address itself is unused, a link-local gateway (what an unnumbered peer usually advertises — `default via fe80::1`, or `default via 169.254.100.0`) and an on-link default route with no gateway at all are both usable here, unlike `DefaultGateway` mode. A peer whose interface cannot be derived yet — normally because the default route is not installed yet — is left unconfigured and logged at Warn once, rather than failing the reconciliation. If the route moves, the session reconciles onto the new interface. An address-less peer also needs plumbing on the agent side, included here: peer status is matched by name rather than by address (an unnumbered peer has no configured address, so address matching silently dropped it from `CiliumBGPNodeConfig` status), the address gobgp resolves is fed back into the route policies keyed on peer address (otherwise nothing is ever advertised to the peer), and `cilium bgp peers` prints the resolved zoned address without a meaningless `:port` suffix before resolution. ### Commits 1. **vendor: bump gobgp to v4.8.0 for unnumbered AddPeer fix.** the gRPC `AddPeer` path rejected interface-only neighbors, fixed upstream in [osrg/gobgp#3504](https://github.com/osrg/gobgp/pull/3504). 3. **fix(bgp): only auto-discover the default gateway from the main table.** Pre-existing `DefaultGateway` bug: a node's other tables carry default routes that are not the way off the node, often at a better metric. 4. **feat(bgp): add peerInterface field for IPv6 link-local peering.** The explicit-address counterpart to unnumbered peering — a `fe80::/10` `peerAddress` plus the interface it is reachable on, yielding a zoned neighbor. 5. **feat(bgp): support BGP unnumbered via autoDiscovery mode Unnumbered.** Routes interface-only peering through `autoDiscovery` rather than a standalone `peerInterface`, per the maintainer steer on #22132. 6. **feat(bgp): send IPv6 Router Advertisements on unnumbered interfaces.** FRR only keeps an unnumbered neighbor whose link-local it learned from that peer's RAs, and gobgp sends none. Also carries a datapath fix — RS/RA were dropped by `snat_v6_nat()` rather than punted to the stack like NS/NA. 7. **feat(bgp): discover the unnumbered interface from the default route.** The `defaultGateway` form of mode `Unnumbered`, described above. Docs for both `Unnumbered` forms, the peer-side requirements (FRR `neighbor <iface> interface remote-as <asn>`, RFC 8950 extended next hop for IPv4 over the IPv6 session), and sample `cilium bgp peers` output are in commits 2 and 6. The CRD schema version is bumped to 1.34.3. ### Testing Unit tests cover the new reconciler paths, CEL validation, conversions, status reporting and the RA reconciler. The end-to-end validation against a live cluster peered with FRR was done not from this branch but from the equivalent work backported to v1.19.x on my fork (`lab-backport-v1.19.4`). This main-targeted branch is the functional twin, adapted for main. The two are kept in deliberate lockstep: - Same behavior, adapted code — not a blind rebase. Each branch is adapted for its gobgp version and table API. - gobgp major version differs. The backport vendors the cilium/gobgp v3 fork (`vendor/.../gobgp/v3/...`) carrying the equivalent unnumbered fixes; main vendors upstream osrg/gobgp v4.8.0, which ships the `AddPeer` fix as released code. v4 keys `neighborMap` by `netip.MustParseAddr(addr)`, which parses the resolved zoned link-local correctly. - Table API rename. main uses `tables.DeviceByName`; the v1.19.x backport still uses `tables.DeviceNameIndex` / `DeviceIDIndex` (rename is main-only). signal.title: BPF masquerade drops IPv6 Router Solicitations and Advertisements on nodes whose masquerade address is a link-local
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version Observed on v1.19.4, but this is not a version-specific bug: the ICMPv6 punt list in `snat_v6_nat()` is byte-for-byte identical in v1.19.4, v1.19.6, v1.20.0 and `main`, so every supported release is affected. I picked the exact-version fields below over the dropdown for that reason rather than to skip the upgrade check. ### What happened? On a node whose only IPv6 address on the selected devices is a link-local, IPv6 Router Solicitations and Router Advertisements emitted by the node are dropped by BPF masquerade: ``` xx drop (Unsupported protocol for NAT masquerade, -1) flow 0x0 , file nodeport_egress.h:152, identity host->unknown: fe80::bae9:24ff:fe80:ebfe -> ff02::1 icmp RouterAdvertisement ``` The chain is: 1. When no selected device has a global IPv6 address, the best IPv6 fallback node address is the link-local itself. `fallbackAddresses.update()` ranks candidates by public-vs-private and scope and does not exclude link-locals, so `bpfMasqAddrs()` hands that link-local to the datapath as `nat_ipv6_masquerade`. 2. RS/RA are always sourced from a link-local, so `__snat_v6_needs_masquerade()` matches such a packet on its very first test — source equals the masquerade address — and answers `NAT_NEEDED`. 3. That leaves `snat_v6_nat()` nothing but the ICMPv6 type to go on: it only consults `snat_v6_nat_can_skip()` for TCP/UDP/SCTP. It punts echo replies, redirects and NS/NA to the stack and returns `DROP_NAT_UNSUPP_PROTO` for everything else, including RS and RA. Expected: RS/RA reach the wire untranslated. Neighbor Discovery is link-local by definition and must never be masqueraded — rewriting an RA's source would advertise the masquerade address as the router's link-local. RFC 4890 §4.4, which 5244b68c1468 ("bpf: Hande icmpv6 in host firewall") cites when it added the NS/NA punt, lists RS/RA in the same must-not-be-dropped group. I hit this doing BGP unnumbered peering, where the node emits RAs out a Cilium-managed native device and the FRR peer will not accept an unnumbered neighbor whose link-local it has not learned from those RAs — but nothing about the drop is specific to BGP; any RA sender on such a node is affected. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Install Cilium with BPF masquerade and IPv6 enabled: `--set enableIPv6Masquerade=true --set bpf.masquerade=true --set ipv6.enabled=true` 2. Use a node where none of the selected devices has a global IPv6 address, only a link-local, so the chosen `nat_ipv6_masquerade` is that link-local. Confirm with `cilium-dbg statedb node-addresses` / the agent's masquerade address in `cilium-dbg status`. 3. Emit an RA out that device from the host netns (radvd, `zebra`, or a crafted packet). 4. `cilium-dbg monitor --type drop` shows the drop above. A BPF unit test reproduces it without a cluster; it ships with the fix as `bpf/tests/host_bpf_masq_linklocal.c` and sets `nat_ipv6_masquerade` to the node's link-local and sends an RA and an RS through the host egress program. ### Cilium Version ``` Client: 1.19.4 go version go1.25.10 linux/amd64 Daemon: 1.19.4 go version go1.25.10 linux/amd64 ``` This is a build off the v1.19.4 tag carrying my in-flight BGP-unnumbered patches from #47394. None of them touch the NAT code — `bpf/lib/nat.h` is stock v1.19.4 here. ### Kernel Version ``` Linux node1 6.17.9-45-g435a44e1-coreweave-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Apr 9 14:24:27 UTC 2026 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux ``` ### Kubernetes Version ``` Client Version: v1.36.3 Kustomize Version: v5.8.1 Server Version: v1.35.4 ``` ### Regression Not a regression — the ICMPv6 punt list in `snat_v6_nat()` has never included RS/RA. It was added for NS/NA in 5244b68c1468. ### Anything else? A fix is on the way; it is being split out of #47394 into its own PR, which I will link here.

signal.title: Improve Conntrack garbage collection
signal.text: The current implementation (as of v1.2) for managing the contents of the datapath connection tracking map leaves something to be desired: Once per minute, the userspace `cilium-agent` makes a series of calls to the `bpf()` syscall to fetch all of the entries in the map to determine whether they should be deleted. For each entry in the map, 2-3 calls must be made: One to fetch the next key, one to fetch the value, and perhaps one to delete the entry. The maximum size of the map is 1 million entries, and if the current count approaches this size then the garbage collection goroutine may spend a significant number of CPU cycles iterating and deleting elements from the conntrack map. We have previously attempted using an LRU map to manage entries, however we hit https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/3239 . Observation was that TCP CT entries would be removed from the table and this would cause traffic disruption for long-lived connections. **EDIT 2019-08**: As of v1.6 (and likely earlier releases) we have resolved some of the LRU issues and are back to using LRU for the primary method of managing conntrack entries. Proposals to address this: 1. ~Build a userspace shadow of CT entries based on monitor events (related: #4080)~ This would reduce the 2-3 syscalls per entry down to 1 syscall for each entry that needs to be deleted. * Ensure that trace messages are generated on datapath add/delete from CT map * Extend messages if necessary to include explicit notification of CT create/delete * Open a monitor socket from `cilium-agent`: * Create an entry in userspace when CT add event is received * Update timer when event is fired for packet allowed to a destination * Delete an entry when CT delete event is received * Periodically iterate over the userspace map and delete entries that have exceeded their timer * Sort CT entries by oldest and only iterate through entries whose timer is in the past 1. Manage CT entries more actively from the datapath * [x] Consider splitting TCP CT map from UDP map (#5501) * [ ] Populate TCP map via socket events * [ ] Replace UDP map GC from userspace with LRU map in datapath (on supported kernels) * [ ] Remove userspace management of CT map

signal.text: Add cookie-based Gateway API session persistence for HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute rules as described in [CFP-47089](https://github.com/cilium/design-cfps/pull/102). Supported session persistence options are validated, with unsupported values being rejected. Accepted routes are ingested into the internal model and translated into CiliumEnvoyConfig. If a Gateway has any attached route rule containing a session persistence config, the Envoy stateful session filter is applied, alongside per-route cookie settings. signal.text: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a Fixes: #XXX line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [x] If your commit description contains a Fixes: <commit-id> tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! BGP peer auto-discovery in defaultGateway mode walks the whole StateDB route table and picks the default route with the lowest metric. The route table is populated from a RT_TABLE_UNSPEC netlink dump, so it holds default routes from every table, not just main — and a default route outside main is not the way off the node. This matters in practice because Cilium installs one itself. With native routing plus any of EnableEnvoyConfig, IPsec, or WireGuard, installFromProxyRoutes* adds default via <cilium_host address> dev cilium_host to table 2005 (RouteTableFromProxy) with no metric, i.e. priority 0. That outranks a real uplink default route, which typically carries a non-zero metric, so auto-discovery hands BGP the cilium_host address as the peer address and the session never comes up. Table 2004 (RouteTableToProxy) similarly holds a local default dev lo; it has no nexthop so it was already skipped, but nothing made that intentional. Restrict selection to unicast routes in the main table, which is where the node's default gateway lives. Non-unicast types (local, blackhole, unreachable, prohibit) do not forward anything either. Test changes: - A new unit case models a node with a metric-1024 main-table default route alongside a metric-0 local default dev lo in table 2004 and a metric-0 default via 10.0.5.160 in table 2005, and asserts the main-table gateway still wins. Existing default routes are built through a small defaultRouteEntry helper so every fixture carries a realistic table and type. - peering-default-gateway.txtar now sets table: 254 / type: 1 on its routes. The fixture previously left both at zero (RT_TABLE_UNSPEC / RTN_UNSPEC), which the kernel never reports for an installed route. release-note Fix BGP `defaultGateway` peer auto-discovery selecting a default route from a non-main routing table, such as the `default via cilium_host` route Cilium installs in the from-proxy table, instead of the node's real default gateway. This PR was prepared with AIL:2. I personally wrote or checked all code and validated the behavior end-to-end against a live cluster and DPU as peer (on the v1.19.x backport).

signal.title: operator/ipam: Remove the per-node pool-maintainer retry trigger
signal.text: Each CiliumNode creates 4 triggers today, and one of them exists only to call another one: the "-retry" trigger's entire body is `poolMaintainer.Trigger()`, rate limited to one call per minute. That is one goroutine and one timer per node, which on a large enough production cluster where the majority of goroutine count is driven by node count, amounts to a quarter of the operator's parked trigger waiters. It exists only because of a skewed invariant. The two halves of `waitingForPoolMaintenance` live in different layers: the enqueue sites set it, and `MaintainIPPool` clears it on the one return path. Its early return for an unstable instances API returns with the flag still set, and the flag makes both `allocationNeeded()` and `releaseNeeded()` false, which gate the only two places that ever enqueue the maintainer. Nothing can re-drive the node, hence the retry trigger. This commit gives the flag a single owner instead. `MaintainIPPool` takes it on entry and releases it with a defer, so it is held for exactly the duration of a pass and released on every return path, and the enqueue sites only enqueue. The node reports its deficit again, so the interval based background resync re-drives it, and since that resync only reaches `Resync()` after a successful instances API resync, the node is picked up in the very iteration that observes the API recovering. While it is down the maintainer is re-triggered by node events rather than once per minute, but each of those is an early return that mutates nothing and is bounded by the backoff already applied to failed maintenance. This also fixes a latent strand on the second early return, taken while the instance has been stopped for less than a minute. Its comment says to wait for the custom resource to be updated as a sign of life, but that wait could never complete: `UpdatedResource()` marks the instance running and then consults `allocationNeeded()`, which was false because the flag was still set. A node that briefly stopped while in deficit stayed stranded until the operator restarted.

The docker-in-docker devcontainer feature fails to install Moby on that release as the package is not available in that ubuntu release. See error: ``` $ devcontainer up --workspace-folder . The 'moby' option is not supported on ubuntu 'resolute' because 'moby-cli' and related system packages are not available in that distribution. 0.082 (!) To continue, either set the feature option '"moby": false' or use a different base image. 0.082 ERROR: Feature "Docker (Docker-in-Docker)" (ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/docker-in-docker) failed to install! Look at the documentation at https://github.com/devcontainers/features/tree/main/src/docker-in-docker for help troubleshooting this error. ``` After this patch: ``` $ devcontainer up --workspace-folder . [...] # suceeds $ devcontainer exec cat /etc/lsb-release DISTRIB_ID=Ubuntu DISTRIB_RELEASE=26.04 DISTRIB_CODENAME=resolute DISTRIB_DESCRIPTION="Ubuntu 26.04 LTS" ``` --- A lot of make targets use `contrib/scripts/builder.sh` to ensure they get executed in the reproducible context of the cilium-builder image. signal.title: CFP: Support dynamic IP address allocation in Cilium Network Driver
signal.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? The Cilium Network Driver proposed in [cilium/cilium#43295](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/43295) and [CFP-43295](https://github.com/cilium/design-cfps/pull/85) can allocate and prepare network devices for Pods through Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). Those devices may also need IPv4 and/or IPv6 addresses, but the Network Driver does not have a scalable way to allocate them dynamically. Requiring a cluster operator to assign static addresses does not scale and is particularly unsafe with reusable `ResourceClaimTemplate` objects: multiple claims created from the same template must not receive the same address. Cilium Pod IPAM modes cannot be used directly because these addresses belong to claimed network resources, not to the Pod's primary Cilium interface, and their allocation lifecycle follows DRA prepare/unprepare operations rather than CNI endpoint creation and deletion. Without dedicated resource IPAM, operators must maintain per-workload address assignments themselves, cannot safely reuse claim templates, and cannot independently manage address capacity for different secondary networks or device classes. ### Describe the feature you'd like Add dedicated IPAM support for the Cilium Network Driver. It should manage addresses for DRA network resources and coexist with any IPAM mode used for Pods; enabling it must not change or consume capacity from Pod IPAM. ### Requirements - Support IPv4-only, IPv6-only, and dual-stack configurations. Allow cluster operators to define the address spaces available to DRA resources, including efficient use of small address ranges. - Support independently managed address spaces for different secondary networks or device classes, and allow each DRA device request to identify its intended address space. Cilium must not silently allocate an address from a different network when the requested address space is unavailable. - Allocate the required address or addresses while preparing a DRA `ResourceClaim`, before the device is configured for the Pod. The allocated addresses must be exposed through the claim's allocated-device status so that the result is inspectable and can be restored. - Make claim operations idempotent. Retrying preparation must preserve the existing allocation rather than consume another address. Cilium component restarts must not change live allocations, and a partially failed preparation must roll back any newly allocated addresses. - Release addresses when the claim is unprepared and they are no longer used. Stale capacity must be reclaimed safely when nodes or claims disappear. - Handle concurrent claims without duplicate live allocations within the same address space. Missing configuration, address-family mismatches, and exhaustion must leave the claim unprepared and surface an actionable, retryable error. - Scale across large node counts and high claim churn without allocation latency or API-server and control-plane load becoming a bottleneck. Unused capacity must be reclaimable safely. - Cover the allocation, retry, restart/restore, rollback, release, exhaustion, IPv4, IPv6, and dual-stack paths with automated tests and document the operational lifecycle. ### Scope and non-goals This issue is limited to IP address management for network devices handled by the Cilium Network Driver. It does not propose changes to device discovery, DRA scheduling, SR-IOV or other device-manager behavior, VLAN or route configuration, NRI integration, or Cilium datapath connectivity for the secondary interface. It also does not replace existing Pod IPAM modes or track static address assignment. ### Notify relevant community channels @cilium/network-driver @cilium/sig-ipam

signal.title: Add various routing fixes for ENI IPv6 support
signal.text: # What is this This PR fixes three issues with IPv6 on ENI. 1. Fixes a bug where if the health check endpoint IP is an IPv6, the ENI specific routing for IPv6 would not be configured. This removes this limitation by filling the routing table for IPv6 health endpoints. 2. When IPSec is enabled on EKS, the pod subnets are determined using the routing info CIDR. Previously only IPv4 CIDRs were parsed. Now both IPv4 and IPv6 pod subnets are filled. 3. When Ingress IP is used with IPv6 enabled, this change makes sure the routing rules are configured similar to how they are configured for IPv4. # Testing For the health check endpoint, I was able to validate that before the fix, on a node with only IPv6 enabled, the main v6 routing table was missing an entry for `lxc_health`. Following the fix, the table now shows the route to the health check endpoint: ```bash 1234:[...]::bded dev lxc_health proto kernel metric 1024 pref medium ``` And curling the endpoint shows it as reachable ```bash curl http://[1234:[...]::bded ]:4240/hello -v * Trying [1234:[...]::bded ]:4240... * Connected to 1234:[...]::bded (1234:[...]::bded ) port 4240 > GET /hello HTTP/1.1 > Host: [1234:[...]::bded ]:4240 > User-Agent: curl/8.5.0 > Accept: */* > < HTTP/1.1 200 OK < Content-Length: 0 < * Connection #0 to host 1234:[...]::bded left intact ``` For the IPSec bug, I couldn't really test it since we don't run this kind of setup. # Release note ```release-note ENI IPv6: Fix IPv6 routing for health check endpoint, ingress address and for IPSec on ENI interfaces. ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:2.

signal.title: Fix: data race for unlocked map read in regeneration goroutine
signal.text: <!-- Description of change --> This is a Go map concurrent read data race bug. The core issue is that a new goroutine is spawned to perform `e.isPropertyLocked()` instead of calling the API on the original goroutine ``` go func() { if !e.isPropertyLocked(endpointtypes.PropertyFakeEndpoint) { e.scrubIPsInConntrackTable() } close(datapathRegenCtxt.ctCleaned) }() ``` e.isPropertyLocked() reads e.properties (a map[string]any) without holding any lock: ``` func (e *Endpoint) isPropertyLocked(propertyKey string) bool { if v, ok := e.properties[propertyKey]; ok { ... } return false } ``` Go maps are not safe for concurrent access. If goroutine A writes e.properties while holding the lock, and this new goroutine reads e.properties without holding the lock, the Go runtime will panic with fatal error: concurrent map read and map write. The fix replaces it with e.IsProperty(), which acquires a read lock first: ``` func (e *Endpoint) IsProperty(propertyKey string) bool { e.mutex.RWMutex.RLock() defer e.mutex.RWMutex.RUnlock() return e.isPropertyLocked(propertyKey) } ``` This ensures all reads of e.properties are properly synchronized. signal.title: feat(endpoint): add managed endpoint table
signal.text: Add a StateDB table for Cilium-managed endpoint metadata. The table is populated from CEP/CES resources and kvstore IPIdentityPair updates, and it stores per-producer source assertions so doublewrite mode can merge equivalent CRD/CES and kvstore entries without guessing by IP, identity, or labels. Kvstore IPIdentityPair metadata now carries the CEP name written by the local endpoint. That gives kvstore entries a semantic bridge back to the CEP/CES endpoint key while preserving the existing global endpoint metadata as an alias for grouping kvstore IPv4/IPv6 entries. This is the first PR in the endpoint-table direction discussed in #46459. It intentionally stops before moving egress gateway onto the table; that consumer change will follow separately once the table shape is reviewed. Preview consumer branch, not an upstream PR: [EGW managed endpoint table consumer](https://github.com/pamelia/cilium/compare/codex%2Fmanaged-endpoint-table...codex%2Fegw-managed-endpoint-preview). The compare is against this PR's branch, so it shows only the follow-up egress gateway consumer changes. Related: #46459 ```release-note Cilium now maintains an internal StateDB table for Cilium-managed endpoint metadata from CEP/CES and kvstore sources. ``` This PR has no direct user-facing behavior change and is labeled `release-note/misc`. This PR was prepared with LLM assistance (AIL:4). I reviewed the resulting diff, kept the scope to the endpoint metadata/table layer, removed environment-specific test data, and ran focused package tests locally. signal.title: gateway-api: ingest validated routes after status handling
signal.text: Move Gateway API ingestion in reconcile to run right before translation and after listener validation and route status processing instead of before them. The change is mostly structural. It makes the sequencing explicit in reconcile and avoids constructing the ingestion model before the status/validation layer has finished producing the inputs that ingestion relies on.
signal.author: mhofstetter

signal.title: gateway-api: add support for ExtensionRef using Envoy ext_proc filter
signal.text: Add support for Gateway API `ExtensionRef` filters backed by a new typed `CiliumEnvoyExtProcFilter` CRD. This lets HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute attach Envoy `ext_proc` filters without requiring users to author raw `CiliumEnvoyConfig`. This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally reviewed each line of the submission. In addition to the Cilium Makefile validations, I ran tests in a live kind cluster that can be found here: https://github.com/eufriction/k8s-cilium-gapi#test-results-by-version. The implementation currently includes: - a namespaced `CiliumEnvoyExtProcFilter` - Gateway API ingestion and translation support for HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute `ExtensionRef` filters - feature-falgs for Helm and operator - ReferenceGrant enforcement and route status reporting for cross-namespace ext_proc backends - Envoy ext_proc metrics - unit/golden-file coverage plus user-facing documentation and examples. Design notes: - Envoy `ext_proc` filters are inserted before `ext_autz`. - I think the best long-term solution is to have a placement strategy with support for First, BeforeAuth, AfterAuth, and Last. This will not be included in this PR until more feedback from the community arrives as @youngnick suggest. - For this PR, Cilium resolves the order using Gateway API precedence: oldest route creation timestamp wins, followed by namespace/name and filter index. - Surfacing conflicts through a Gateway API status condition is not done yet. Could maybe wait for #46681? - Unresolved or invalid ext_proc BackendRefs fail closed. The affected route receives a configuration error and a 500 DirectResponse Fixes: #45951 ```release-note Gateway API HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute filters can reference CiliumEnvoyExtProcFilter resources via ExtensionRef to configure Envoy ext_proc filters. ```
signal.author: eufriction

signal.title: loader: prune global functions unreachable from live code
signal.text: On pre-6.8 kernels the BPF verifier independently verifies every global function (GLOBAL BTF linkage) in a program, even when the only call sites to that function are in dead code eliminated by our reachability analysis. This prevents maps referenced solely within those functions from being pruned: removeUnusedMaps poisons their map loads, but the verifier's independent pass then rejects the poisoned load. Fixes: #45918 ```release-note loader: prune global functions unreachable from live code ``` [AI Influence Level]: Lvl 1 (The wording of some comments are modified by AI.)

signal.title: bpf/tests: minor fix ups
signal.text: When starting to build out BPF tests for netkit, it became apparent that there were a few data issues between pktgen-based packets and scapy-defined packets. 1. pktgen sets TCP seq/win values in host byte order, meaning calculated TCP checksums are wrong. This becomes a problem when you migrate a packet definition to scapy, which sets correct byte order, and thus the correct TCP checksum values. 2. pktgen's `default_data` string includes a NUL-terminating character, but scapy's does not. This leads to packet lengths being different, and causes differences in L3 checksum values. This commit fixes these issues and updates all affected tests to include new checksum values. ```release-note Fix byte ordering of TCP fields in BPF integration tests. ```
signal.author: ajmmm

signal.title: l2announcer: leader-election Lease name is a plain namespace+name concatenation, so two Services can end up sharing one Lease
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? L2 announcements derive the per-Service leader-election Lease name by gluing the namespace and the Service name onto a prefix with a hyphen, and a hyphen is legal inside both halves. Two unrelated Services can therefore map onto the same Lease name and end up in one leader election. ```go const leasePrefix = "cilium-l2announce" Name: fmt.Sprintf("%s-%s-%s", leasePrefix, svc.Name.Namespace(), svc.Name.Name()), ``` https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/ee26050851a92746155a7319b2554054adb0966c/pkg/l2announcer/l2announcer.go#L847-L860 Namespace `foo` + Service `bar-baz`, and namespace `foo-bar` + Service `baz`, both produce `cilium-l2announce-foo-bar-baz`. There is no sanitization, escaping or hashing anywhere on that path; the only other place the name is touched is the GC scan, which just prefix-matches (`strings.HasPrefix(lease.Name, leasePrefix)`) and does not disambiguate either. Same code on v1.19: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/44d55ea770e38bdf4b3a5f5d8079ab311f5a4911/pkg/l2announcer/l2announcer.go#L820-L826 Expected: one Lease per Service. ### Mechanism ### Impact Needs a hyphen in the right place, so it is not going to be common, but it is silent when it happens and the symptom points at the L2 policy rather than at a name collision. Multi-tenant clusters where namespaces are generated with a prefix (`team-a`, `team-a-staging`) and Service names are equally hyphenated are where I would expect it. ### Suggested fix Use a separator that cannot appear in either half. Neither a namespace (DNS-1123 label) nor a Service name (DNS-1035 label) may contain `.`, and `.` is legal in an object name (DNS-1123 subdomain), so `fmt.Sprintf("%s-%s.%s", leasePrefix, ns, name)` is unambiguous and stays readable in `kubectl get leases`. A hash suffix would also work but costs readability. Either way the name changes on upgrade, which orphans the existing Leases. Those are released on agent shutdown (`ReleaseOnCancel`), which empties the holder identity, and `leaseGC` already deletes prefix-matching Leases with an empty holder, so the old objects should clean themselves up. I have not confirmed that. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Enable L2 announcements and a `CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool`. 2. `kubectl create namespace foo && kubectl create namespace foo-bar` 3. Create Service `bar-baz` of type LoadBalancer in `foo`, and Service `baz` of type LoadBalancer in `foo-bar`. 4. Create `CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy` objects selecting both, with disjoint `nodeSelector`s so the two Services are announced from different nodes. 5. `kubectl get leases -n kube-system | grep cilium-l2announce` shows one Lease named `cilium-l2announce-foo-bar-baz` instead of two. ### Cilium Version N/A — found by source inspection, no live cluster involved. ### Kernel Version N/A — found by source inspection, no live cluster involved. ### Kubernetes Version N/A — found by source inspection, no live cluster involved. ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: gateway-api: an apiserver 500 during CRD discovery is treated as "CRDs not installed", disabling Gateway API for the lifetime of the operator
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? Follow-up to #43130 (fixed by #43452 and #44662). Those fixes handle the case where the apiserver is unreachable at the network level. This report is about the remaining hole: an apiserver that answers, but answers 500. `cilium-operator` started while etcd was going through a leader election. The Gateway API CRD discovery GET came back as a server-side error, the operator logged the "resources are not found" message and moved on with Gateway API off. No retry, no backoff warning, no restart. The pod then ran for two hours without a single further gateway-related log line, and the GatewayClass kept the default `Accepted=Unknown / Pending / "Waiting for controller"` status that the upstream CRD ships. Deleting the operator pod fixed it immediately. The CRDs were installed the whole time. The operator said they were not. Expected: a transient server-side failure is retried like a transient network failure, and if it does not clear, the operator exits so the kubelet restarts it. Only a real "the CRD is absent" answer should disable Gateway API silently. ### Mechanism `discoverCRDsWithRetry` splits every discovery failure into "retry" and "the CRDs are not installed" using `isTransientError`, and the second branch is the default: - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/ee26050851a92746155a7319b2554054adb0966c/operator/pkg/gateway-api/cell.go#L162-L169 - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/ee26050851a92746155a7319b2554054adb0966c/operator/pkg/gateway-api/cell.go#L365-L388 `isTransientError` is an allowlist: four `k8serrors` predicates (`IsServerTimeout`, `IsServiceUnavailable`, `IsTooManyRequests`, `IsTimeout`) plus four `syscall.Errno` values. A 500 carrying `Reason: InternalError` matches none of them, and that is exactly what the apiserver returns when the storage layer fails: `Internal error occurred: etcdserver: leader changed`. Neither does a bare 500 with no reason (`IsUnexpectedServerError`), nor a transport error that is not a plain `syscall.Errno`, such as `http2: client connection lost` or a `Client.Timeout` wrapped in `*url.Error`. Nothing upstream of that narrows it either. `checkCRDs` joins raw client errors, and `CheckCRD` returns the client error untouched; `NotFound` is never distinguished from anything else: - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/ee26050851a92746155a7319b2554054adb0966c/pkg/k8s/client/crd.go#L15-L37 So the branch that is supposed to mean "the operator looked and the CRD is genuinely absent" is reached by every failure mode the allowlist does not name, and its effect is permanent: `Enabled: false` is returned to the hive, `registerReconcilers` never runs, and no watch, timer or health probe re-enters the path. v1.19 is the same code, verified on the v1.19.7 tag: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/44d55ea770e38bdf4b3a5f5d8079ab311f5a4911/operator/pkg/gateway-api/cell.go#L170-L177 ### Impact Any cluster where the control plane can return a server-side error for a second or two at operator startup. Managed and self-hosted control planes move etcd leadership during upgrades, node replacement and maintenance; the operator is restarted at exactly those moments. The failure is silent — the operator is Running and Ready, the message points at installation docs for CRDs that are already installed, and nothing recovers without a manual pod delete. ### Suggested fix Invert the default. Retry unless the error is specifically `k8serrors.IsNotFound`, i.e. treat "the CRD object does not exist" as the only permanent answer and everything else as retryable. That also removes the need to keep extending the allowlist for every new error shape. If the allowlist stays, it needs at least `IsInternalError` and `IsUnexpectedServerError`, plus a `net.Error` check for transport errors that do not carry an `Errno`. Either way the message on the permanent branch should be reworded: "resources are not found" is what sent me to check the CRDs first, and they were fine. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Install the Gateway API CRDs and enable `gatewayAPI.enabled=true`. 2. Make the apiserver return 500 for `GET /apis/apiextensions.k8s.io/v1/customresourcedefinitions/gatewayclasses.gateway.networking.k8s.io` for a few seconds during operator startup. Losing the etcd leader is the natural way; an admission webhook or a proxy that injects 500 works too. 3. Start `cilium-operator` into that window. 4. `kubectl get gatewayclass cilium -o yaml` stays at `Accepted=Unknown`, and the operator log has exactly one gateway line after the discovery message. It never recovers. ### Cilium Version v1.19.5 (vendored chart; behavior verified identical on the v1.19.7 tag) ### Kernel Version 6.18.38 (Talos v1.13.6) ### Kubernetes Version v1.35.6 ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell level=info msg="Checking for required and optional GatewayAPI resources" requiredGVK="[gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1, Kind=gatewayclasses ...]" level=error msg="Required GatewayAPI resources are not found, please refer to docs for installation instructions" error="etcdserver: leader changed" The absence of the `"Failed to check GatewayAPI CRDs due to transient error, will retry"` warning is the tell: the backoff loop was never entered, the error went straight down the permanent branch on the first attempt. ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: envoy: Clarify legacy UpdateEnvoyResources

signal.title: gha: bound the LLVM prereq apt step with a 5m timeout
signal.text: In run 32225900868 the "Install LLVM and Clang prerequisites" step of build-commits-test hung inside apt-get for 2h51m and only stopped because the run was cancelled by hand. The step has no bound of its own, so the only thing that would have ended it is the job's timeout-minutes: 180, which burns nearly three hours of an extra-power runner before the PR reports anything. Across the last successful Build Commits runs the step completes in 6 to 18 seconds, so 5 minutes leaves plenty of headroom for a slow mirror while still failing fast when apt wedges. A hung apt is not something a retry inside the step can recover from, so failing the job and letting it be re-run is the right outcome. This PR was prepared with AIL:3.

signal.title: ipam/eni: Source the ENI VPC CIDRs from IMDS
signal.text: Today every ENI's status carries its VPC's CIDRs (`status.eni.enis.[].vpc`). But all ENIs for a given node can only belong to a single VPC, the node's VPC, so there is unnecessary duplication in having the VPC properties be present on each ENI's status. But in addition to that, we don't even need this to be in the `CiliumNode` CRD at all. Today the operator makes AWS EC2 API calls to get VPC CIDRs, then writes them to each ENI's status on the `CiliumNode` and the agent watches those on startup and waits to see them populated by the operator. The operator never reads those, only the agent needs them. And the agent doesn't even need the operator to get them. The agent already queries its node's IMDS for some node properties (including its VPC ID), we can just extend this IMDS-based facts gathering to get the agent the VPC CIDRs (which are available via IMDS). That way the agent no longer needs to wait for the operator to write those in the `CiliumNode` and the operator no longer needs to make AWS API calls to regularly fetch VPC properties. This PR implements the first half of that: update the agent to read the VPC CIDRs from the IMDS instead of from the operator-populated `CiliumNode`. The operator continues to fetch VPC data and write it to the `CiliumNode`, this is now advertised as deprecated and will be removed with cilium 1.22. See each commit message for details. Some tracing views of how the new IMDS-backed VPC CIDRs discovery fits in the agent bootstrap phase:

signal.title: Fix 5-tuple collision in conformance kind proxy embedded
signal.text: Fix test flake due to 5-tuple collision. The flake happens in `l7-lb` test that intentionally accesses the same backend via both L7-LB service and normal L3/4 load balancer service when the pod happens to use the same source port for both: 1. Access via L7-LB service works, Envoy keeps the upstream connection open on the 5-tuple with the source pod IP/port and the backend IP/port 2. Access via non-L7-LB service stalled due to CT entry keeping the `from_l7lb` flag from the previous L7-LB upstream connection, causing SYN/ACK to be redirected to Envoy. This is fixed by the bpf datapath change in the first commit. 3. Access via L7-LB service again fails due to the backend not having consistent TCP connection state with the Envoy upstream connection that is still open on the Envoy end. This is fixed by enabling retry timeouts and setting socket linger option to 0, causing the old upstream connection being closed synchronously after the timeout, so that the retry connection can re-use the same 5-tuple and negotiate a new connection with the backend This was confirmed in a local test that explicitly set the same source port for `curl`. AIL: 3 ```release-note Set `envoy.httpRetryTimeout` to one second and `envoy.httpUpstreamLingerTimeout` to zero to recover from 5-tuple collisions between L7-LB and non-L7-LB traffic. ```

signal.title: Host firewall: policy-selected node is permanently isolated after reboot — host endpoint policy map ends up deny-all (cold boot, audit-off flip) or allow-all (runtime label add), never the computed policy
signal.text: ## Is there an existing issue for this? Closest match is #25448 ("host firewall drops reply traffic for legitimate connections when policies are first enforced"). This report is a stronger manifestation of what looks like the same enforcement-transition problem: in our setup the drop window is not transient — it is fatal and self-sustaining (node permanently isolated until out-of-band reboot), it reproduces on every cold boot, and it also reproduces on a fully synced agent when audit mode is switched off at runtime. Filing separately because the evidence points at the host endpoint's BPF policy map never receiving the computed allow entries, with three distinct end states depending on the path taken. ## What happened? Environment: Cilium 1.18.6 (kubespray), host firewall enabled, kube-proxy replacement enabled, VXLAN tunnel, WireGuard node encryption, `bpf-datapath-mode: netkit`, CRD identity mode, 61 nodes. A `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` with `nodeSelector` on worker nodes provides ingress lock-down (fromEntities cluster/remote-node/health/host, SSH/ICMP via CiliumCIDRGroup refs plus literal CIDRs, kubelet/NodePort from cluster). **1. Cold boot of a selected node → permanent isolation.** ~13 s after cilium-agent starts, every packet in and out is dropped as `Policy denied` by `bpf_host.c:865`. The node never recovers: the agent needs the apiserver to finish its sync, and its own egress to the apiserver is what is being dropped. Captured from inside a locked node (systemd unit dumping via crictl exec): - at agent start, `cilium-dbg endpoint list` is still **empty** (host endpoint not created yet) while bpf_host is already attached and enforcing deny-by-default with an empty policy map; - 105 659 `Policy denied` drops in 20 s, 73 018 of them the node's own egress to the apiserver LB: `identity host->unknown: <node-ip>:* -> <apiserver-lb-ip>:6443`; - at that moment the BPF ipcache is fully populated (8 292 entries) and local CIDR identities for the policy's allowed CIDRs are already allocated — e.g. ICMP from an explicitly allowed CIDR is dropped with its allocated identity (`identity 16777222->unknown`). The policy is computed; its allow entries are just not in the host endpoint policy map. **2. Runtime audit-off flip on a fully synced agent → same isolation.** Boot the node with `policy-audit-mode: true` (per-node CiliumNodeConfig): node comes up healthy, host endpoint reaches `state=ready`, realized policy has all 8 L4 ingress rules, `enforcement=audit-ingress`. Then `cilium-dbg endpoint config <hostep> PolicyAuditMode=Disabled` → "configuration updated successfully" → the node is fully isolated within seconds. The agent log ends abruptly mid incremental `UpdatePolicyMaps` processing with no error line — consistent with the deny default being installed while the allow entries never land. **3. Warm enforcement via label add → policy map silently allow-all.** With the agent fully synced and the node label added at runtime (CCNP starts selecting the node), the endpoint reports `enforcement=ingress`, but `cilium-dbg bpf policy get <hostep>` contains only the wildcard pair (`Allow Ingress ANY` prefix 0 / `Allow Egress ANY` prefix 0) — i.e. no actual enforcement. This is the only transition that leaves the node reachable, and it appears to do so by not programming the policy at all. For contrast, a long-running node whose agent processed the CCNP incrementally while already enforcing has a fully programmed map (per-identity allows, port ranges) — so the policy→map pipeline itself works. So the same policy, same version, produces three different host endpoint policy-map end states depending on the transition path: deny-all (cold boot, audit-off flip), allow-all (runtime label add), correct (incremental update on an already-enforcing endpoint). Datapath mode does not appear to matter: a cold boot with `bpf-datapath-mode: veth` (per-node CiliumNodeConfig) locked out identically (caveat: the override's application could not be positively confirmed from inside the locked node). Impact: any reboot of a policy-selected node isolates it permanently; recovery requires out-of-band console/rescue access. 54 nodes affected in our cluster. ## Cilium Version 1.18.6 ## Kernel Version 6.8.0-124-generic (Ubuntu 24.04) ## Kubernetes Version v1.33.7 (kubespray) ## Sysdump Not attached (production cluster); can provide targeted captures on request. Full monitor drop capture (17 MB) and repeated boot-time snapshots of `endpoint list` / `bpf policy get` / `bpf ipcache list` from inside a locked node are preserved. ## Relevant log output ``` xx drop (Policy denied) flow 0x... to endpoint 0, ifindex 7, file bpf_host.c:865, , identity host->unknown: <node-ip>:39186 -> <apiserver-lb-ip>:6443 tcp SYN xx drop (Policy denied) flow 0x... to endpoint 0, ifindex 2, file bpf_host.c:865, , identity 16777222->unknown: <allowed-admin-ip> -> <node-ip> icmp EchoRequest ``` Agent start with audit mode (the boot that survives): ``` level=warn msg="PolicyAuditMode is enabled. Network policy will not be enforced." level=info msg="Regenerating restored endpoints" restored=0 level=info msg="Creating host endpoint" ``` ## Anything else? - The reboot lockout window matches #25448's "first enforcement" semantics; unlike #25448 the state is permanent because the dropped traffic includes the agent's own apiserver path (chicken-and-egg). - Feature combination overlaps with #31209 (tunnel + KPR + WireGuard + host firewall). - Nothing relevant found in 1.18.7–1.18.13 changelogs. - Happy to run instrumented builds / additional captures on a dedicated test node. ## Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: gha: authenticate release images with OIDC
signal.text: Use OIDC to authenticate the release image build to quay.io and Docker Hub, instead of the static passwords for both. Quay needs the exchange spelled out, because a GitHub signed token is not accepted as a registry password there, so it is traded for a short lived robot token first, the same way build-images-ci.yaml does it since #47742. Docker Hub handles it inside docker/login-action, which asks for an ID token and exchanges it on its own identity endpoint when a connection ID is set and no password is given. The job already references the release environment, so the token subject is repo:cilium/cilium:environment:release. That is not the subject the CI images use, so the release robot needs its own federation entry on the Quay side before this can run. This PR was prepared with AIL:3.

signal.title: renovate: Fix primary GID of the ubuntu user and restore builder.sh root check
signal.text: ## Summary The `ubuntu` user in `ghcr.io/renovatebot/renovate` is defined with primary GID 0: ```console $ docker run --rm ghcr.io/renovatebot/renovate:43.176.5 grep ubuntu /etc/passwd ubuntu:x:12021:0::/home/ubuntu:/bin/bash ``` so Renovate and everything it spawns run as `12021:0`, and `builder.sh` takes the temporary root path added in #45663 instead of its normal UID/GID remapping. ## Changes **1. Swap the ubuntu user's primary group before dropping privileges** (`.github/actions/renovate/entrypoint.sh`) ```sh if [ "$(id -gn ubuntu)" = "root" ]; then usermod -aG root ubuntu usermod -g ubuntu ubuntu fi ``` Renovate then runs as `12021:12021`, with root kept as a supplementary group. **2. Create `/home/ubuntu/.cache` in the builder container before chowning it** (`contrib/scripts/builder.sh`) When no cache directory gets mounted (e.g. Go is not installed on the host, as in the Renovate image), `/home/ubuntu/.cache` doesn't exist and the unconditional `chown` fails under `set -eu`. A `mkdir -p` before the `chown` fixes this for every caller. **3. Remove the temporary root workaround and block root explicitly** (`contrib/scripts/builder.sh`) With the GID fixed, the workaround from #45663 is no longer needed. Running with UID or GID 0 now fails early, so an accidental root run can't reassign GID 0 files inside the container. ## Testing Verified end to end with a live Renovate run on a fork, using this branch's entrypoint and `builder.sh`, without `BUILDER_GOCACHE_DIR`. The genuine `postUpgradeTask` on the `renovate/all-go-deps-main` branch ran `contrib/scripts/builder.sh true` to completion: - `runuser -u ubuntu -- id` → `uid=12021(ubuntu) gid=12021(ubuntu) groups=12021(ubuntu),0(root),118(docker_group)` - `builder.sh` took the normal UID/GID remapping path (the new root check never fired), `mkdir -p /home/ubuntu/.cache` ran, and the `chown` that used to fail succeeded; rc=0. This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally verified the container group membership behavior and the end-to-end Renovate runs described above. Fixes: #45663 ```release-note Fix the Renovate entrypoint to run with the ubuntu group instead of GID 0, and restore builder.sh's rejection of root. ```

signal.title: Gateway API: intermittent fixed ~5.02s stall before request is proxied upstream (v1.19.4, VXLAN, no node encryption)
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? # Gateway API: intermittent fixed ~5.02s stall before request is proxied upstream (v1.19.4, VXLAN, no node encryption) ## Summary Requests through a Gateway API listener intermittently stall for a fixed **~5.02 seconds** before the request is proxied to the backend. The backend never sees the request during the stall. Envoy reports no timeouts, retries, or circuit-breaker events, and there is no 5s value anywhere in the effective Envoy config. No requests are lost — with a client timeout above 5s everything completes successfully. Reproducible across four independent clusters. Rate correlates **inversely** with node count, which we cannot explain. ## Environment - Cilium **v1.19.4**, cilium-envoy **v1.36.6** - Gateway API, `kube-proxy-replacement=true` - `routing-mode=tunnel` (VXLAN), jumbo MTU (`cilium_vxlan` 9001, `cilium_wg0` 8921, physical NIC 9001) - `enable-wireguard=true` with **`NodeEncryption: Disabled`** - Managed Kubernetes on AWS, arm64 (Graviton) nodes; Amazon Linux 2023, kernel `6.12.88-119.157.amzn2023.aarch64` - Gateway fronted by an internal L4 load balancer (instance targets, cross-zone enabled, client-IP preservation on) Relevant cilium-config values (no 5s among them): ``` proxy-connect-timeout: 2 proxy-idle-timeout-seconds: 60 http-stream-idle-timeout: 300 proxy-initial-fetch-timeout: 30 gateway-api-service-externaltrafficpolicy: Cluster ``` Effective Envoy config timeouts (from `/config_dump`): `idle_timeout 60s`, `stream_idle_timeout 300s`, `connect_timeout 2s`, `initial_fetch_timeout 30s`, plus `600s`/`900s` route timeouts. **No 5s value.** ## Symptom Client is a pod in-cluster calling an HTTPS hostname routed to the internal Gateway. `curl` timing on a stalled request: ``` total=5.024006 time_appconnect=0.023203 time_starttransfer=5.023998 code=000 ``` TLS completes normally (~23ms), then nothing for ~5.0s. The stall lands at 5.02s regardless of client timeout: | Client timeout | Result | | --- | --- | | `--max-time 5` | 28/30 | | `--max-time 20` | 28/30, the 2 slow ones at **5.025s** and **5.024s** | | `--max-time 30` | **60/60 complete**, 7 slow | Raising the client timeout does not move where the stall lands, so this is not client impatience. ## The backend never receives the request during the stall Backend has a **single replica**, so the backend node is constant and only the Envoy node varies per request. `tcpdump` in the backend pod's netns, correlated with per-request timings. For a request that stalled from `02:18:48.8` to `02:18:53.9`, the backend received **zero packets** for the whole window — the next SYN to `:8080` arrives at `02:18:53.944`, i.e. only after the stall clears: ``` 02:18:48.764381 In IP <envoy-a>.46017 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... 02:18:48.802412 In IP <envoy-b>.42843 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... 02:18:48.838080 In IP <envoy-a>.44405 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... 02:18:48.874295 In IP <envoy-c>.32887 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... ... 5 SECOND GAP, nothing to the backend ... 02:18:53.944994 In IP <envoy-d>.45869 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... ``` Largest inter-packet gaps on the backend side were `5.066s` and `5.056s`, matching the stalls. Client-side capture of a stalled vs a succeeding connection — byte-identical until the request, then: | | Success | Stalled | | --- | --- | --- | | request (`len 136`) sent | `39.480903` | `39.519219` | | next activity | `39.492036` (**+11ms**) | `44.518844` (**+5000ms**) | So the request is sent and ACKed at TCP level, but not proxied upstream for ~5s. ## The backend is never slow ``` cluster...<backend>_8080.upstream_rq_time: P0=4ms P50=6.0ms P90=7.1ms P99=9.1ms P100=9.1ms ``` Max upstream request time across 90 requests: **9.1ms**. ## Envoy reports no timeout of any kind Zero on all of: `upstream_rq_timeout`, `upstream_rq_retry`, `upstream_rq_per_try_timeout`, `upstream_cx_connect_timeout`, `upstream_cx_overflow`, `circuit_breakers`. No listener `downstream_cx_overflow`, no `downstream_pre_cx_timeout`, no overload-manager activity. Counters that did move over a 60-request run with 7 stalls: | Counter | Value | | --- | --- | | `upstream_cx_idle_timeout` | 44 | | `upstream_cx_destroy_local` | 44 | | `upstream_cx_total` | 47 | | `upstream_rq_per_cx` | P50=2.0 | | `downstream_cx_delayed_close_timeout` | 2 | | `upstream_rq_pending_total` | 41 → 47 | We initially suspected upstream connection-pool churn from this, but **ruled it out**: another cluster with the *lowest* stall rate (~2%) idle-reaps **100%** of its upstream connections (e.g. 103 requests over 102 connections) versus 94% here. Higher churn, lower stall rate — so aggressive idle-reaping appears to be normal behaviour and is not the mechanism. ## Only via the Gateway | Path | Result | Stalls | | --- | --- | --- | | Internal Gateway | 28/30 at 5s timeout | 2 | | k8s Service (`http://svc:8080`) | **30/30** | **0** | | Direct pod IP | **20/20** | **0** | ## Rates across four clusters (5s client timeout, so these are stall rates) | Cluster | Relative node count | Internal Gateway | External Gateway | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A | largest (~4.5x smallest) | ~2% | 0% | | B | ~2.2x smallest | ~6% | 0% | | C | smallest | ~18% | 0% | | D | smallest | ~11% | 0% | Cilium version, cilium-envoy version, cilium-config, Gateway API config, load-balancer and target-group attributes, Envoy coverage, MTU, and pod/service CIDRs are identical across all four. **External** Gateway listeners in the same clusters are unaffected (0%). The inverse correlation with node count is consistent but unexplained. It is not a bad AZ or a bad LB node — pinning each load-balancer IP individually gives a uniform rate (2, 3, 2 stalls out of 25 each). ## Ruled out (with evidence) load-balancer target health · Gateway API config · load-balancer/target-group attributes · BPF rate limiting · connection reuse and idle timeout · ALPN · cilium datapath drops (`cilium-dbg monitor --type drop` captured 0 during a live failure) · Hubble drops · Envoy `no_filter_chain_match` · Envoy protocol errors · listen-queue overflow · node churn/age · Envoy coverage · cilium version/config differences · WireGuard · MTU · CIDR collision · client DNS (`time_namelookup` is 1.5ms on stalled requests; `ndots:5` search-path expansion investigated and excluded) · `wireguard-persistent-keepalive=0s` (stalls persist under continuous back-to-back load, including consecutive stalls) · upstream connection-pool churn (see above) · TCP RSTs observed in-pod (they appear on successful requests too — ordinary client teardown) ## Notes on related issues - #40428 (v1.18 hardcoded 5s `connectTimeout`) — fix shipped in v1.19.0; we are on v1.19.4 and our `connect_timeout` is `2s`, so this is not it. - #32592 — we already run `encryption.enabled: true` + `encryption.type: wireguard`, the workaround reported there, and still stall. That report is hostNetwork + VPC-CNI chaining with 100% cross-node failure; ours is intermittent, no hostNetwork. - #46100 — enabling `encryption.nodeEncryption: true` on one cluster took our stall rate from ~12% to **100%**, matching #46100's conditions (VXLAN + node encryption, NIC MTU 9000, `wg0` 8921, v1.19.3+). We reverted. Note this is a **separate** problem: with node encryption disabled we see **no fragmentation drops at all** (`cilium_ipv4_frag_datagrams` untouched, no `DROP_FRAG_NOT_FOUND`), yet the ~12% stall persists. ## What would help Any pointer to what, in the Gateway API path, could defer proxying an already-accepted request by a fixed ~5s without incrementing any Envoy timeout counter. We are happy to run further captures or provide a sysdump. ### How can we reproduce the issue? ## Reproduction / methods used Packet capture inside a pod (streaming via `kubectl debug -it` was unreliable for us; write to a file and read via `kubectl logs`): ```bash kubectl -n <ns> debug <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot:latest --target=<container> -q -- \ bash -c 'tcpdump -i any -nn -S -tttt "tcp port 443" > /tmp/c.txt & sleep 3; <drive traffic>; kill -INT %1; <analyse>' kubectl -n <ns> logs <pod> -c <debugger-name> ``` Envoy admin stats from a node (no curl in the envoy/agent images): ```bash curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/cilium/envoy/sockets/admin.sock http://localhost/stats ``` The Envoy listener port for a Gateway changes on reconfiguration — read it from `/listeners` rather than hardcoding. ### Cilium Version **Environment** - Cilium `v1.19.4`, cilium-envoy `v1.36.6` - `routing-mode=tunnel` (VXLAN), `kube-proxy-replacement=true` - Managed Kubernetes on AWS, **arm64** (Graviton) nodes - Jumbo frames: physical NIC `9001`, `cilium_vxlan` `9001`, `cilium_wg0` **`8921`** ### Kernel Version - Amazon Linux 2023, kernel `6.12.88-119.157.amzn2023.aarch64` ### Kubernetes Version - Managed Kubernetes 1.35 on AWS, **arm64** (Graviton) nodes ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct
